entities.name: Grand Mosque
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Grand Mosque of Mecca (also called Al-Masjid al-Haram in some contexts, but here referring to the expanded official complex as a whole), or more specifically mosques titled 'Grand Mosque' in other Muslim capitals, represents the architectural expression of Islamic state power and community gathering. In its most common non-Meccan usage, 'Grand Mosque' typically refers to the Umayyad Mosque of Damascus, the Great Mosque of Cordoba, or the Hassan II Mosque of Casablanca — each expressing its era's peak of Islamic architectural ambition.

The Hassan II Mosque in Casablanca (completed 1993), designed by French architect Michel Pinseau, is the world's seventh-largest mosque and the tallest religious structure in Africa — its 210-meter minaret (the world's tallest) is a laser beam projecting toward Mecca each night. Built on a promontory over the Atlantic Ocean at King Hassan II's command ('God's throne was built on water'), 40% of its floor is retractable glass over the ocean. It cost $585 million, with most funding from Moroccan citizen contributions.

The Mosque of Cordoba (Great Mosque of Cordoba, 784-987 CE) — commissioned by Abd al-Rahman I on the site of a Visigothic church — represents the peak of Andalusian Islamic architecture: 856 columns creating a 'forest of columns' effect, a mihrab with Byzantine mosaics commissioned from Constantinople, and a bicolor red-and-white horseshoe arch system that became definitive of Moorish style. The subsequent Christian conversion to a cathedral (1236 CE) created the unique architectural hybrid that UNESCO protects today.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Islamic architectural tradition of Grand Mosques — from Cordoba's 856-column forest to Hassan II's Atlantic promontory minaret — represents 1,400 years of Islamic states expressing political legitimacy through sacred architectural ambition.
